title: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Library
shortTitle: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Library
summary: Archiving via library replaces the external archiving program with compression or encryption code linked directly into the attacker's own process. Libraries such as rarfile for Python, libzip, and zlib provide the same functions a utility would, but they are called as functions inside the running program instead of being launched as a separate child process. That single difference changes the entire telemetry picture. There is no process creation event naming an archiving binary, no command line and no arguments to read, no shell history entry, and nothing for a rule that watches for tar, zip, or makecab to match. What remains is the result on disk and whatever the host process itself did: a new archive file appearing in a staging directory, a spike of file writes across a set of collected documents, and possibly high entropy output if encryption was applied. On Unix like systems, bzip2 and zip support may already be present as shared objects, and on Windows the zip support is part of the operating system, so again nothing unusual needs to be installed. Detection therefore leans on file system telemetry, integrity and inventory checks, and memory or module analysis that spots well known compression code loaded into a process that has no business archiving anything. The correlation to hunt for is a process that writes many files and then produces a single large or high entropy file followed by outbound network activity.

beginner.definition: This is the version of data packing that uses a code library instead of a separate program. A library is a bundle of ready made functions that a program can call while it runs. The attacker's own software calls those functions to compress or encrypt stolen files. It differs from the parent technique only in how the packing is done. That one change hides a lot of evidence.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most detection rules watch for archiving programs being started. Here no program is started at all, so those rules stay silent. There is no command line to read and no shell history to review, which removes the easiest clues. A defender is left with the file on disk and the process that created it. If you only look at process names, you will not see this happen. You need file and memory visibility as well.
howItWorks: The attacker's code already has the gathered files inside the machine it controls.
Instead of starting an archiving program, it calls functions from a linked library.
Those functions compress the data and can also encrypt it into one output file.
Because the library runs in the same process, no child process appears in logs.
The output file lands in a staging folder, ready for the next stage of theft.
Defenders must rely on file creation records, file entropy, and loaded code in memory.
beginner.example: Imagine an office worker who needs to pack a parcel. One way is to walk to the post office and use its machine. Everyone can see that machine from the window. The other way is to use a small folding machine kept in a desk drawer. The parcel looks the same when it is finished. But nobody saw the worker leave a desk, and no queue record exists. Only the finished parcel on the counter tells you what happened.
takeaways: A linked library packs data inside the running process, so no tool is started.
With no process event to match, detection shifts to files, entropy, and memory.
A new high entropy archive written outside backup folders deserves a closer look.

objectives: Explain the difference between an archiving utility and an archiving library.
Describe why library based archiving removes process creation evidence.
Identify the file system artefacts that remain when a library performs the archiving.
Explain why encrypted output from a library can look random and how entropy helps analysts.
Compare detection options for this sub-technique against the utility based sub-technique.
Describe how memory or module inspection can spot compression code in an unexpected process.
